notes.definition: Environmental changes, such as changes in temperature, the availability of water and the composition of atmospheric gases, affect where species are found (their distribution) in an ecosystem. These changes can be natural or caused by human activity.
explanation: The distribution of a species is where it is found. Every species can only survive and reproduce within a certain range of conditions, because its adaptations suit those conditions. If the environment changes, an area may become unsuitable for a species that lived there, or suitable for a species that could not live there before. The species may then die out locally, move away, or spread into new areas. This means environmental change alters the distribution of species and can change the whole community in an ecosystem.

Temperature is one of the main factors. As average temperatures rise, many species are found further towards the poles or higher up mountains, where conditions are now cool enough for them. Species that need cold conditions can lose habitat because there is nowhere colder left to move to, for example at the top of a mountain. Warmer conditions also allow some species from warmer regions to spread into areas where winters used to be too cold for them, for example some insects and birds that have spread north in Britain in recent decades.

The availability of water also affects distribution. Changes in rainfall patterns, droughts, flooding and the draining of wetlands all change which species can survive in an area. Plants such as reeds and animals such as amphibians need wet habitats, so they disappear if an area dries out. Drought-tolerant species may spread into areas that become drier. Rivers and lakes that shrink or dry up remove habitats for fish and invertebrates.

The composition of atmospheric gases matters too. Some lichens are very sensitive to sulfur dioxide, so few lichen species are found near sources of this gas, such as cities and industrial areas, and more species are found where the air is cleaner. Increasing carbon dioxide and methane concentrations contribute to global warming, which changes temperature and rainfall and so affects distribution indirectly. Higher carbon dioxide concentration can also change how fast plants grow.

Environmental changes can be natural or caused by humans. Natural causes include volcanic eruptions (which release gases such as sulfur dioxide and ash), long-term climate cycles, and changes in ocean currents that affect rainfall. Human causes include burning fossil fuels, deforestation, draining wetlands, irrigation and building dams. In the exam you may be given data, such as a map, graph or table, and asked to evaluate the impact of an environmental change on the distribution of a species. A good evaluation describes the pattern in the data, links it to the change, considers other factors that could be responsible, and comments on whether the evidence is strong enough (sample size, time period, correlation rather than proof of cause).
keyFacts: Distribution means where a species is found in an ecosystem.
Environmental changes that affect distribution include temperature, availability of water and composition of atmospheric gases.
Changes may be natural (for example volcanic eruptions) or due to human activity (for example burning fossil fuels).
As temperatures rise, many species shift towards the poles or to higher altitudes.
Cold-adapted species on mountain tops may have nowhere left to move to.
Drying out of wetlands or changes in rainfall change which plants and animals can live in an area.
Many lichen species cannot survive in air with high sulfur dioxide concentrations.
A correlation between an environmental change and a change in distribution does not prove the change caused it.
This whole subtopic is Higher tier and separate Biology only.

keyTerms.definition: Where a species is found within an ecosystem or across a region.
A change in the non-living conditions of an ecosystem, such as temperature, availability of water or the gases in the atmosphere.
A non-living factor that affects a community, such as temperature, moisture levels or carbon dioxide concentration.
A species whose presence, absence or abundance shows the level of a particular pollutant or condition, such as lichens for sulfur dioxide.
Height above sea level. Temperature generally falls as altitude increases.
A change in the area where a species is found, for example moving further north or higher up a mountain.
A link between two variables, where one changes as the other changes. It does not by itself prove that one causes the other.

equations.name: Percentage change
equations.formula: percentage change = (new value − original value) ÷ original value × 100

workedExamples.title: Percentage change in the number of sites
workedExamples.question: A species of butterfly was recorded at 120 sites in northern England in 1995. By 2020 it was recorded at 186 sites. Calculate the percentage change in the number of sites.
steps: The value is positive, so this is a 55% increase.

workedExamples.title: Rate of a range shift
workedExamples.question: The northern edge of the range of a dragonfly species moved 147 km further north between 1990 and 2011. Calculate the mean rate of movement in km per year.

workedExamples.title: Evaluating a claim from data
workedExamples.question: Scientists found that the lowest altitude at which a mountain plant grows rose from 1600 m to 1720 m over 40 years, while the mean summer temperature rose by 1.2 °C. Evaluate the claim that rising temperature caused the change.
steps: Describe the pattern: the plant now grows 120 m higher up (a lower limit shift of 3 m per year).
Link to the change: temperature falls with altitude, so warming makes lower slopes too warm for a cold-adapted plant; the shift is in the expected direction.
Consider other factors: grazing, changes in rainfall, competition from other plants spreading uphill or changes in land use could also be responsible.
Comment on the evidence: data from one mountain and one species is limited; a correlation does not prove cause. Repeating the study on other mountains would make the conclusion more valid.
workedExamples.answer: The data support the claim because the shift is in the direction expected from warming, but other factors may be involved and more data would be needed to be confident.

diagrams.title: Species moving uphill as temperature rises
diagrams.caption: Temperature falls as altitude increases. When the climate warms, the band of altitude that suits a cold-adapted species moves higher, so the species' distribution shifts uphill and its area shrinks.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think animals choose to migrate to new areas because they decide it is too hot.
misconceptions.right: In fact, a distribution changes because individuals survive and reproduce better in some areas than others. Populations increase where conditions now suit them and decrease where they no longer do.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all environmental changes are caused by humans.
misconceptions.right: In fact, changes can be natural, such as volcanic eruptions releasing sulfur dioxide or natural climate cycles, as well as caused by human activity.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a correlation in the data proves the environmental change caused the change in distribution.
misconceptions.right: In fact, a correlation only shows a link. Other factors such as competition, predation, disease or land use may also explain the change.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think warming always increases the number of species in an area.
misconceptions.right: In fact, warming may let some species move in but may force cold-adapted species out, so the community changes and biodiversity may fall.

realWorld: Many species of butterfly and dragonfly in Britain have been recorded further north than they were a few decades ago, which ecologists link to warmer temperatures.
Lichens are used as indicator species to monitor air quality, because sensitive species disappear where sulfur dioxide levels are high.
Draining wetlands for farming has removed the habitats of wading birds, amphibians and wetland plants in many areas.
Large volcanic eruptions release sulfur dioxide and ash that can cool the climate for a year or more and damage vegetation nearby.
higherTier: The whole of this subtopic is Higher tier only: environmental changes affect the distribution of species in an ecosystem.
The changes include temperature, availability of water and composition of atmospheric gases, and may be due to natural or human causes.
Higher tier students should be able to evaluate the impact of environmental changes on the distribution of species when given appropriate information.
separateOnlyContent: This subtopic (4.7.2.4) is only in separate Biology (8461). It is not part of Combined Science Trilogy (8464).
examTips: When asked to evaluate, give points for and against the claim and finish with a conclusion that is supported by the data.
Always quote figures from the data (with units) when describing a change in distribution.
Say which environmental factor has changed (temperature, water or atmospheric gases) and explain how it affects survival or reproduction of the species.
Mention that correlation does not prove causation and suggest other factors that could explain the pattern.
For percentage change, divide the change by the original value, not by the new value.
summary: Environmental changes affect the distribution of species.
Key changes: temperature, availability of water and composition of atmospheric gases.
Changes can be natural or caused by human activity.
Warming often shifts species towards the poles or uphill.
Lichen species are fewer where sulfur dioxide levels are high.
Evaluate data by describing the pattern, linking it to the change and considering other factors and the strength of the evidence.

flashcards.front: What does the distribution of a species mean?
flashcards.back: Where the species is found in an ecosystem or region.

flashcards.front: Name the three environmental changes in the AQA spec that affect species distribution.
flashcards.back: Temperature, availability of water and composition of atmospheric gases.

flashcards.front: Give one natural cause of environmental change.
flashcards.back: For example a volcanic eruption, natural climate cycles or changes in ocean currents.

flashcards.front: Give one human cause of environmental change.
flashcards.back: For example burning fossil fuels, deforestation, draining wetlands or building dams.

flashcards.front: How does warming usually affect the distribution of species?
flashcards.back: Many species shift towards the poles or to higher altitudes.

flashcards.front: Why are cold-adapted mountain species at risk from warming?
flashcards.back: Their suitable zone moves uphill and shrinks; at the summit there is nowhere colder to move to.

flashcards.front: Why are lichens useful for showing air pollution?
flashcards.back: Many lichen species cannot survive high sulfur dioxide concentrations, so their absence shows polluted air.

flashcards.front: How can a change in water availability affect distribution?
flashcards.back: Droughts or drained wetlands remove species that need wet conditions; drought-tolerant species may spread in.

flashcards.front: Does a correlation prove an environmental change caused a change in distribution?
flashcards.back: No. Other factors such as competition, predation, disease or land use could be responsible.

flashcards.front: Is 'impact of environmental change' in Combined Science?
flashcards.back: No. It is separate Biology only and Higher tier only.

flashcards.front: What makes evidence about distribution changes more valid?
flashcards.back: Large samples, many sites, long time periods, repeat surveys and controlling or recording other variables.

questions.question: What is meant by the distribution of a species?
options: The number of individuals of the species in an area
The rate at which the species reproduces
markScheme: 1 mark: where the species is found
questions.explanation: Distribution describes where a species is found. The number of individuals in an area is population size or abundance, not distribution.

questions.question: Which of these is an environmental change named in the AQA specification as affecting the distribution of species?
markScheme: 1 mark: availability of water
questions.explanation: Temperature, availability of water and composition of atmospheric gases are the abiotic changes named. Predators, disease and competitors are biotic factors.

questions.question: Which of these is a natural cause of environmental change?
options: Building a dam across a river
markScheme: 1 mark: a volcanic eruption
questions.explanation: Volcanic eruptions release gases such as sulfur dioxide and ash without human involvement. The other three are human activities.

questions.question: As the average temperature of a region rises, in which direction would a cold-adapted species on a mountain most likely move?
options: It would not move at all
markScheme: 1 mark: uphill to higher altitude
questions.explanation: Temperature falls with altitude, so the cooler conditions the species needs are now found higher up. Moving towards the equator would take it into warmer conditions.

questions.question: Lichen species are rarely found close to a city centre. Which gas is most likely to explain this?
markScheme: 1 mark: sulfur dioxide
questions.explanation: Many lichens are very sensitive to sulfur dioxide, an acidic gas from burning fossil fuels. Oxygen, nitrogen and water vapour do not harm lichens.

questions.question: A species of insect is now found 200 km further north than it was 30 years ago. Which statement best explains this?
options: Individual insects decided to fly north to escape the heat
Warmer winters mean more insects survive and breed further north
The insects evolved to prefer cold weather
Northern areas now have fewer plants
markScheme: 1 mark: warmer winters allow more insects to survive and breed further north
questions.explanation: Distribution changes because populations survive and reproduce in new areas when conditions there become suitable. Insects do not make decisions about climate, and evolving to prefer cold would not explain a northward shift into warming areas.

questions.question: A farmer drains a wet meadow. Which group of organisms is most likely to disappear from the meadow?
markScheme: 1 mark: frogs and reeds
questions.explanation: Amphibians such as frogs need water to breed and reeds grow in waterlogged soil, so drying the meadow removes their habitat. The other organisms can live in drier grassland.

questions.question: A study shows that as carbon dioxide concentration rose over 50 years, the range of a bird species moved north. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Carbon dioxide directly kills the birds in the south
The data prove carbon dioxide caused the range shift
Carbon dioxide has no effect on any species
There is a correlation, but other factors may also have caused the shift
markScheme: 1 mark: there is a correlation, but other factors may also be involved
questions.explanation: A correlation between two variables does not prove cause. The effect of carbon dioxide on birds is likely to be indirect, through warming, and other factors such as land use or food supply could also explain the shift.

questions.question: Which change to a study would most improve the validity of a conclusion that warming caused a plant to move uphill?
options: Recording the plant on the same single slope more often in one year
Recording the plant on many mountains over many years and recording other variables such as grazing
Measuring the height of the tallest plant only
Using a different colour of quadrat
markScheme: 1 mark: many mountains over many years, also recording other variables
questions.explanation: Many sites over a long time give a larger, more representative sample, and recording other variables helps rule out alternative causes. More visits to one slope in one year would not show a long-term trend.

questions.question: The number of sites where a species of dragonfly was recorded rose from 40 in 2000 to 58 in 2020. Calculate the percentage increase.
questions.explanation: Percentage change = change ÷ original × 100 = 18 ÷ 40 × 100 = 45%. Dividing by 58 instead of 40 gives 31%, which is wrong because you must divide by the original value.

questions.question: The number of lichen species on gravestones in a churchyard fell from 48 to 30 after a factory opened nearby. Calculate the percentage decrease.
questions.explanation: The decrease is 18 species. 18 ÷ 48 = 0.375, so the percentage decrease is 37.5%.

questions.question: The lower edge of the range of a mountain hare moved from 450 m to 570 m above sea level over 40 years. Calculate the mean rate of movement in metres per year.
markScheme: 1 mark: 120 ÷ 40 = 3 m per year
questions.explanation: The edge rose by 120 m in 40 years, so the mean rate is 120 ÷ 40 = 3 metres per year.

questions.question: A beetle species occupied 2500 km² of a region. After a long drought its area of distribution fell by 18%. Calculate the new area of distribution.
markScheme: 1 mark: 18% of 2500 = 450 km²
questions.explanation: 18% of 2500 = 0.18 × 2500 = 450 km². The new area is 2500 − 450 = 2050 km². Alternatively, 0.82 × 2500 = 2050 km².

questions.question: Look at the lichen graph in the notes. At 5 km from the city centre there are 3 lichen species and at 15 km there are 18 lichen species. Calculate the percentage increase in the number of species between 5 km and 15 km.
questions.explanation: The increase is 15 species. 15 ÷ 3 = 5, so the percentage increase is 500%. Percentage increases can be greater than 100% when the value more than doubles.

questions.question: Over 25 years the mean annual temperature at a site rose from 9.2 °C to 10.4 °C. A plant's northern range edge moved 90 km north during the same period. Calculate how far the range edge moved for each 1 °C rise in temperature.
markScheme: 1 mark: temperature rise = 10.4 − 9.2 = 1.2 °C
1 mark: 90 ÷ 1.2 = 75 km per °C
questions.explanation: The temperature rose by 1.2 °C. Dividing the distance by the temperature rise gives 90 ÷ 1.2 = 75 km for each degree. The 25 years is not needed for this calculation.

questions.question: State one human activity that changes the composition of atmospheric gases.
markScheme: 1 mark: any one, for example burning fossil fuels, deforestation or cattle farming (methane)
questions.explanation: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide; deforestation releases carbon dioxide and cattle and rice fields release methane.

questions.question: Give two natural causes of environmental change that could affect the distribution of species.
markScheme: 1 mark: first natural cause, for example volcanic eruption
1 mark: second natural cause, for example natural drought or a change in ocean currents
questions.explanation: Natural causes do not involve humans. Volcanic eruptions change atmospheric gases, and natural climate cycles and ocean currents change temperature and rainfall.

questions.question: Name the type of organism often used as an indicator of sulfur dioxide air pollution.
markScheme: 1 mark: lichen(s)
questions.explanation: Many lichen species cannot survive in air with a high sulfur dioxide concentration, so the number of lichen species shows how clean the air is.

questions.question: Explain why many species are now being found further north in Britain than they were 50 years ago.
markScheme: 1 mark: average temperatures have risen (global warming)
1 mark: northern areas are now warm enough for the species to survive and reproduce, so populations become established there
questions.explanation: Warming means conditions in the north now fall within the range the species can tolerate, so populations can survive the winter and breed there.

questions.question: Explain how a long period of drought could change the distribution of plant species in a river valley.
acceptedAnswers: plants that need wet soil die
markScheme: 1 mark: water availability falls / soil dries out
1 mark: species that need wet conditions die or are lost, and drought-tolerant species survive or spread in
questions.explanation: Water availability is one of the key environmental factors. Plants adapted to wet soil cannot survive, while species adapted to dry conditions outcompete them and spread.

questions.question: Suggest why a cold-adapted plant that lives near the summit of a mountain is at greater risk from global warming than a plant that lives at the bottom of the mountain.
markScheme: 1 mark: the zone of suitable (cold) conditions moves higher up the mountain
1 mark: the plant near the summit has nowhere higher (colder) to move to, so its habitat disappears
questions.explanation: A lowland plant can shift uphill, but at the summit there is no colder area left. The area at higher altitude is also smaller, so the population shrinks.

questions.question: A scientist found fewer lichen species on trees close to a main road than on trees 2 km away. Suggest three other factors, apart from air pollution, that the scientist should keep the same or record to make the comparison valid.
markScheme: 1 mark each, up to 3: tree species/bark type; light intensity or shade; height on the trunk; age of the tree; moisture or humidity; direction the trunk faces
questions.explanation: Lichen growth depends on several abiotic factors. If these differ between the sites, they could explain the difference in species rather than the pollution.

questions.question: Data show that the population of a wading bird in an estuary fell by 60% over 20 years, during which sea levels rose and a new marina was built. Evaluate the claim that rising sea levels caused the decline.
acceptedAnswers: sea level rise floods feeding areas
markScheme: 1 mark: rising sea level could cover mudflats used for feeding, so it is a plausible cause
1 mark: the marina could also have removed habitat or caused disturbance
1 mark: conclusion: the data cannot show which factor caused the decline (correlation is not causation); more data are needed, such as comparing estuaries without marinas
questions.explanation: Two changes happened at the same time, so the data alone cannot separate their effects. A good evaluation weighs both and suggests how to find out which matters more.

questions.question: Describe how changes in temperature, availability of water and the composition of atmospheric gases can each affect the distribution of species in an ecosystem. Give an example for each.
markScheme: Indicative content: temperature: warming shifts species towards poles or uphill; cold-adapted species lose habitat; warm-adapted species spread in; water: drought or draining of wetlands removes species needing wet conditions (reeds, amphibians); flooding or more rainfall favours wetland species; gases: sulfur dioxide reduces lichen species near cities; carbon dioxide and methane increase global warming and so change temperature and rainfall.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear description of all three changes, each with a relevant example and a link to survival or reproduction.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one or two changes with little explanation or no examples.
questions.explanation: Top answers link each change to whether organisms can survive and reproduce in the new conditions, and support each with a named example.

questions.question:
In a region of upland Britain, the mean summer temperature rose by 1.5 °C between 1970 and 2020. Over the same period, a survey showed that a species of cold-adapted beetle disappeared from 35% of the low-altitude sites where it had been found, while the number of high-altitude sites where it was found increased slightly. Large areas of the lower slopes were also planted with conifer forests during this time.
Evaluate the claim that the change in temperature caused the change in the distribution of the beetle.
markScheme: Indicative content for the claim: the beetle is cold-adapted; warming makes low-altitude sites too warm; temperature falls with altitude so cooler conditions now only at higher altitude; pattern (loss at low altitude, gain at high altitude) is what warming would predict; 1.5 °C is a substantial rise over 50 years.

Indicative content against the claim: conifer planting on lower slopes changed the habitat (shade, food, soil), which could explain the losses; correlation does not prove causation; other factors such as pesticides, predators, competitors or rainfall changes not recorded; survey methods may have changed over 50 years; sample size of sites not stated.
Improvements: compare low-altitude sites with and without conifer planting; study other mountains; laboratory tests of the beetle's temperature tolerance.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): balanced evaluation using the data, with points for and against, including the confounding effect of conifer planting, and a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some points for and against, with some use of the data, but conclusion missing or weakly justified.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example that warming makes it too hot, with no evaluation.
questions.explanation: The pattern fits warming well, but the conifer planting happened on exactly the slopes where the beetle was lost, so it is a confounding variable. A justified conclusion is that warming is a likely contributor but the data cannot prove it was the cause.

questions.question: Lichens can be used to monitor air quality. Explain how a student could use lichens to compare air quality at two sites, and how the results would show which site had more sulfur dioxide pollution.
markScheme: Indicative content: choose trees or walls of the same type at each site; use a quadrat or grid of fixed size at the same height and on the same side; count the number of different lichen species or estimate percentage cover; repeat on several trees at each site and calculate a mean; fewer lichen species (or only tolerant species) indicates more sulfur dioxide; more species, including sensitive ones, indicates cleaner air.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear method with control of variables and repeats, and a correct interpretation linking fewer lichen species to higher sulfur dioxide.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): basic idea of counting lichens at two sites, with limited detail or interpretation.
questions.explanation: Lichens act as indicator species. Comparing like with like (same surface, height and aspect) and taking repeats makes the comparison fair, and the number of species reflects the sulfur dioxide level.

questions.question: Suggest why an increase in the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere could change the distribution of plant species, even though carbon dioxide is not toxic to plants.
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas that contributes to global warming
1 mark: so temperature (and rainfall) patterns change, making some areas unsuitable and others suitable for particular species
questions.explanation: The main effect of carbon dioxide on distribution is indirect: it raises temperatures and alters rainfall, which changes where species can survive.
